title: I spent a night in Britain's most haunted village - and the 'Screaming Woods' left me terrified
excerpt: We went ghost hunting in Britain’s most haunted village and were left seriously spooked.
content:
Pluckley is known as Britain’s most haunted village. But I wanted to find out whether it could give me a real-life fright.

Spending the night at a haunted farm, dinner at a spooky pub and a trip into the Screaming Woods at witching hour - what could possibly go wrong?

My boyfriend and I stayed at Elvey Farm, which dates back to the 15th century, where owners Nick Leggett and Sonja Johnson run a bed and breakfast from the converted stable block.

The five guest suites have been thoroughly refurbished, but the farm’s history is still part of its appeal. Its most famous ghost story is tied to Edward John Brett, who took his own life at Elvey Farm in 1900. The old dairy and the farm’s grounds are said to be haunted by his spirit.

However, the farm and surrounding fields looked lovely in the autumn sunshine.

A devilish dinner

We headed to the Black Horse pub for dinner just before dusk. It was already heaving with ghost hunters.

We both had a burger, shared a cheesecake and, rather aptly, my boyfriend washed it all down with a Witchcraft Ale.

We got chatting to bartenders Alice Welch, 40, and James Ramsden, 35, who are used to paranormal investigators dropping in. Alice has worked at the pub for about a year and has lived in Pluckley for 13. James, who is from Little Chart, had been bartending there for about four and a half months.

They told us about footsteps and stomping upstairs, a white figure seen in a mirror and child-height shapes by the fire exit. Alice even said that the spirit of a little girl called Emily tugs at her clothes and touches her arms and hair while she works.

Alice, unfazed by the pub’s paranormal activity, took us upstairs to show us its bedrooms and living areas, along with a creepy dolls’ house. She told us about previous landlords sitting on a bed and seeing the impression of someone sitting down beside them.

She also showed us a recording from one of her attempts to communicate with the dead. In it, a scarf appears to move by itself.

Then there was the story of a glass flying off a shelf, hitting Alice on the hip and smashing on the floor. A figure has reportedly appeared on CCTV walking from the car park into the restaurant, while a paranormal investigator is said to have heard a gasp in the attic.

As Alice led us towards the attic, I noticed my chest felt a little tight. Was it the dust, the nerves or something else? I couldn’t tell.

With stories of invisible children, phantom roommates and flying glassware, the pub was doing a good job of setting the mood. I didn’t see anything myself, but I was beginning to understand why ghost hunters keep coming back.

The creepy churchyard

We wrapped up warm and headed to St Nicholas’ Church, just a short walk from the pub. The churchyard is associated with the Red Lady, said in local legend to be a member of the Dering family searching for her stillborn baby.

Darkness had settled over the village, so we switched on our head torches and went in search of our first ghost. The church dates mainly from the 13th and 14th centuries, and its ancient gravestones made the perfect setting.

The churchyard was busy with ghost tours and groups hoping to catch a glimpse of something. Our torches swept over the old gravestones, casting long shadows across the paths. It was certainly eerie, but unfortunately no ghost made an appearance.

The Screaming Woods

Hoping to have better luck elsewhere, we headed to Dering Wood, better known as the Screaming Woods.

It sits just outside Pluckley and is said to echo with blood-curdling screams.

Our head torches lit only a narrow stretch of path, their beams disappearing into the trees. I called out to ask if anyone was there. No answer. Then came a sharp crack as a twig snapped nearby. We stopped and listened. Nothing. A few moments later, another twig snapped, deeper among the trees. We were standing still. It definitely wasn’t us.

I didn’t hear any screams, but the deeper we went, the more I found myself straining to catch every sound. So we turned off our torches.

There were no streetlights, no passing cars and no lights in the distance. Just blackness, stillness and the sound of our own breathing. For a moment, it felt as if the whole wood had gone quiet around us. Then another twig cracked.

I couldn’t see what had made the sound. I couldn’t tell how far away it was. I called out again, but nothing answered. I can’t say a ghost was there, but standing in that darkness, waiting for one to reply, was more than enough to make my imagination run wild.

Still a little jumpy, we hurried back to the car and headed to our home for the night, Elvey Farm.

The frightening farmhouse

But we weren’t quite finished ghost hunting: Nick and Sonja had given us permission to explore the old farmhouse, where Nick had once felt a presence.

He told us that one evening, at about 11pm, when he was walking from the lounge into the back room of the farmhouse: “As I went through the doorway, my hair stood on end and I really felt a presence. I didn’t see anything and I didn’t smell anything, as some people say they have done, or hear anything. But I really felt that something was in the room with me.”

Sonja had her own strange experience in the Oast House.

One Sunday morning, she and Nick had been gardening outside while their daughter Jessie was upstairs. When they came back in for coffee, the television was on. They called up to Jessie, thinking she had left it on, but she said she hadn’t been downstairs.

“It was Easter Sunday and it was actually playing Casper the Friendly Ghost, which we thought was hysterical. So we take it that they’re friendly.”

Sonja had heard unsettling stories from guests, too. Two women staying in the end room asked her the next morning whether anyone had been walking outside during the night. They said they had heard footsteps, as if someone were walking over floorboards. But the ground outside is paved with Yorkstone or gravel.

Another guest told her they had woken in the night after hearing a door creak. The man said he felt someone grab him around the waist and try to pull him out of bed. But there was nobody there. After they left, Sonja tried the doors herself and couldn’t make any of them squeak.

With those stories in mind, we headed into the old farmhouse during witching hour to look for signs of Edward Brett. The building was being restored, and once the daylight had gone, stepping inside felt very different from hearing the stories in the afternoon.

There were no lights and no sounds. In the darkness, all I could hear was the blood rushing in my ears. I couldn’t stop thinking that Brett had died right where I was standing.

But we saw nothing, which was a relief, but also a little disappointing.

An unsettling sleep

Then it was time for bed. Our room was gorgeous, and the amenities were top-notch. I thought I might struggle to find anything scary to focus on.

That was before I turned out the lights.

The room was completely dark: no little red light from the television, no sliver of brightness around the blinds, nothing. My brain started playing tricks on me. Was that a noise? Had something moved? Or was I simply lying in a dark room thinking about all the ghost stories I’d heard?

I kept remembering what Sonja had told me about a guest who said he’d felt arms wrap around him and pull him out of bed. So I left the bathroom door open, letting in a thin strip of light. Thankfully, that was enough to help me get to sleep.

I didn’t feel anything else unusual at the farm, and I had a lovely stay.

But the silence felt different once I knew the stories attached to the place.
